feedback: If a learner tries to cut 3:5 into 3 or 5 segments, point out the two children's parts together must fill the whole strip: 3 + 5 = 8 segments, so neither 3 nor 5 can be the total.
If they answer '5 and 5' after 40 ÷ 8 = 5, respond: 'That is the value of ONE part — how many parts does each child have?' and prompt the final multiply, then the add-back check 15 + 25 = 40.

If they say the 3-part child gets 3/5 of the sweets, have them count the segments on the bar: the denominator is the TOTAL number of parts, so it is 3/8. Contrast 3/8 with 3/5 explicitly, then test the wrong rule on its own terms — if the 3-child got 3/5, by that same rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two shares would be 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 of the sweets, more than the whole, which is impossible. That is why the denominator must be the total, 8.
If they share equally (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each), return to the bar: 3:5 means one child's part is bigger, so the numbers of segments are not equal.
If they treat 'twice' and 'three times' as unrelated, make Jo one part, so Sam is 3 parts and Tom is 6; the total is 10 parts and one part = 3 (for a 30 total). Build the 1:3:6 bar before sharing.
activities.intendedInsight: The ratio a:b needs (a+b) equal parts, so each share is a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the whole — not a/b. One part is the building block; chained comparisons must become a single ratio before sharing.
learnerActions: Take a ratio such as 3:5 and draw an empty strip (a tape/bar diagram) to represent the whole quantity.

Decide how many EQUAL segments to cut the strip into so that both children's parts together fill it exactly (try 3, 5 or another number and check), then explain in your own words why the sum 3 + 5 = 8 is the simplest count that works.
Place the total quantity (40) across the strip and work out the value of one segment: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
Colour 3 segments for the first child and 5 for the second, then read off 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 5 = 25.
State what fraction of the WHOLE each child gets: 3/8 and 5/8, and check these sum to 1 (and that 15 + 25 = 40).

In a second round, turn chained language ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam, Sam three times as many as Jo') into one ratio Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6 by making the smallest quantity one part, then build that 10-part bar before sharing.
activities.title: Cut the sharing bar into the right number of parts

feedback: Correct full response: 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5, shares are 15 and 25 (which sum to 40), and the 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.
If the add-back does not reach 40, a part value or a multiply was wrong — recount segments and recompute one part.

On the 3/8-vs-5 test: 2/5 is the CORRECT complement of 3/5 (3/5 + 2/5 = 1), so 'they fit the whole' does NOT excuse the 3/5 error. Apply the misconception's own rule instead — it treats the 5-child's number of parts (5) as if it were the total, giving the 5-child 5/5, so 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 exceeds the whole. That contradiction shows the denominator must be the total number of parts, 8, giving 3/8 and 5/8.
For the chained problem with 30: one part = 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so Jo = 3, Sam = 9, Tom = 18 (which sum to 30).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding the shares back to the original total is a fast self-check, and articulating why the denominator is the sum of parts secures the part-to-whole fraction and the handling of chained comparisons.
learnerActions: Answer: how many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5, and where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? Say what it would tell you if they did not.

You said the fraction is 3/8 — why is 8 on the bottom and not 5? Test the wrong rule on its own terms: if the 3-part child got 3/5, then by that same rule the 5-part child would get 5/5 (all of them) — do 3/5 and 5/5 fit inside one whole?
Given 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo, 30 altogether', turn it into one ratio (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6) before sharing, and find each share.
activities.title: Explain and check the shares

feedback: For 'share 40 in 3:5', the shares are 15 and 25; an answer of 20 and 20 is equal sharing that ignores the ratio.

For the fraction, 3/8 is correct; 3/5 wrongly uses the other child's number of parts (5) as the denominator instead of the sum of parts. By that wrong rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two 'shares' (3/5 and 5/5) would exceed the whole — a quick sign the denominator must be the sum of parts, 8, not 5.
For a chained problem, first state the single ratio (e.g. 1:3:6) — the multipliers are related, not separate.
activities.intendedInsight: Separating the share values from the part-to-whole fraction lets the learner spot and discard the 'equal share' and 'a/b of the total' errors.
learnerActions: Share 40 in the ratio 3:5 and write the two shares.
Choose what fraction of the whole the '3' child gets.
Read a chained-comparison problem and state the combined single ratio before working out the shares.
